analysis.one_liner: Separates deposit banking from securities trading, swaps, and insurance under a restored Glass-Steagall wall.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote in the House; with 13 cosponsors, it sat in the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees until the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the wall between commercial banking and Wall Street that Congress removed in 1999. Banks holding federally insured deposits could no longer own or be affiliated with securities firms, insurance companies, or swaps dealers, and their executives could no longer hold those jobs at the same time. National banks could take deposits, make loans, and run payment systems, but not underwrite securities, make markets, run hedge funds or private equity funds, trade for their own account, or invest in structured or synthetic products. Existing combinations would have up to five years to unwind, with an anti-evasion rule and a penalty of 10 percent of a violator's three-year average net profits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. Money held in federally insured checking and savings accounts could no longer back the trading desks of universal banks, and the implicit taxpayer guarantee for firms seen as 'too big to fail' would shrink. Bank customers would get advisors whose pay does not depend on pushing them into products the bank itself profits from.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any insured depository institution from being an affiliate of, or under common ownership with, an insurance company, securities entity, or swaps entity, so federally backed deposits cannot be entangled with trading risk [S2] [S3].

Bars national banks from underwriting securities, investing in structured or synthetic products, and limits securities dealing to purchases and sales strictly for customers' accounts, never the bank's own [S2] [S3].
Prohibits bank holding companies from proprietary trading, market-making, prime brokerage, and owning or sponsoring hedge funds or private equity funds [S2] [S3].

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that let financial holding companies mix banking with insurance, securities, and commodities trading, and repeals bankruptcy safe harbors that gave swaps and repo counterparties priority over other creditors [S2] [S3].

Adds an anti-evasion rule with an enforcement duty: regulators must order violators to unwind, impose a penalty of 10 percent of the entity's average net profits over three years, and publish annual public reports naming entities that tried to evade the ban [S2] [S3].
Requires written, under-penalty-of-perjury attestation from bank holding company executives that they are not engaged in prohibited activities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest diversified Wall Street banks — the firms that combine deposit banking with underwriting, market-making, proprietary trading, and swaps dealing — would have to spin off or sell major businesses within five years, costing shareholders and cutting into fee income. Their customers could also see bundled services and some financing products disappear.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large universal banks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Forcing existing combinations to unwind within five years would be a major transition for firms like the big universal banks, with costs likely passed to shareholders and possibly customers in the form of fees or lost one-stop services [S2] [S3].

Critics have long argued a new Glass-Steagall would not have prevented 2008, since the firms that failed — Lehman Brothers, AIG, Bear Stearns — were not insured commercial banks, so the bill's crisis-prevention claim rests on contested analysis of its own findings section [S3].

The bill narrows what national banks may do far beyond the original Glass-Steagall line — banning even structured products and much principal investing — which its opponents would say restricts legitimate services banks can offer customers [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: smaller profits for the biggest banks in exchange for deposit insurance and the taxpayer safety net not standing behind trading desks. The risk-transfer case is strong — the bill's own findings cite federal reports on conflicts of interest and government-insured deposits funding risky bets. But the five-year forced divestiture is a blunt instrument, the claim that it would have prevented the last crisis is contested because the major failures were uninsured institutions, and the transition costs would be real. On balance, a defensible risk reduction, though broader than strictly needed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services and Judiciary Committees on introduction, sent to a Financial Services subcommittee in January 2014, and never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Tierney, a Democrat from Massachusetts, introduced the bill on December 11, 2013, joined by Representative Walter Jones, a North Carolina Republican [S3].
The Speaker referred it to both the Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee, a dual referral that gives each committee only the pieces within its jurisdiction [S5].
On January 27, 2014, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
The bill ended the 113th Congress with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats, 1 Republican), no committee vote, and no floor vote [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal banks, which kept the ability to mix insured deposits with trading, underwriting, and swaps dealing — and the fee income and implicit 'too big to fail' support that come with it. No competing wall was enacted in this Congress either.

industries.industry: Large universal banks (firms combining insured deposits with securities and swaps dealing)
industries.note: The bill would have forced these firms to end affiliations between insured depositories and their securities, insurance, and swaps businesses within five years, eliminating the deposit-subsidized trading model. Its gain for the public — deposits and the taxpayer safety net no longer behind trading risk — is exactly these firms' loss.

industries.industry: Securities underwriting and market-making desks within bank holding companies
industries.note: National banks and bank holding companies could no longer underwrite issues or make markets, ending a major revenue line. The bill's conflict-of-interest rationale is that this revenue was partly earned at customers' expense.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: Bank holding companies could no longer own, sponsor, or invest in them, cutting off a source of capital. Their services would remain legal, just not bank-owned.
Insured depositories could not affiliate with or be commonly owned with insurance companies, unwinding bank-insurer combinations created after Gramm-Leach-Bliley.
Banks could not be swaps entities and bank holding companies could not deal in exchange-traded or over-the-counter swaps, though plain hedging as an end user remains permitted.

The bill's restrictions fall on deposit-taking institutions engaged in securities and swaps activities, not on plain deposit-and-lending banks, which keep a level competitive field and the same deposit guarantee without subsidizing rivals' trading.
